query: For multicomponent high-entropy alloys in solid and liquid states at and near their high melting temperatures, what single testable methodological intervention could overcome the inability of EAM references to represent the many atomic configurations of the ab initio liquid? Explain why it should improve reference–target phase-space overlap, predict the reduction in thermodynamic-integration path mismatch relative to TOR-TILD’s EAM references, define the applicable composition and temperature ranges, identify supporting evidence from elemental or binary calculations, and specify a decisive free-energy benchmark that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A deep neural network (DNN)–based interatomic potential, trained on a diverse set of ab initio liquid configurations for high-melting high‐entropy alloys, will serve as a superior reference in thermodynamic integration calculations compared to traditional EAM potentials, by enhancing phase-space overlap and thereby reducing the integration-path mismatch.
generation.material_initial_state: Multicomponent high-entropy alloys (e.g., refractory HEAs) in both their solid and liquid states at temperatures near melting (approximately 0.9Tm to Tm).
generation.intervention: Develop and employ a deep neural network potential trained on extensive ab initio data covering the wide array of atomic configurations characteristic of the liquid phase; then use this DNN potential as the reference in a TOR-TILD style thermodynamic integration protocol.
generation.conditions: Simulations or experiments conducted under high-temperature conditions (around 0.9–1.0Tm) in controlled atmospheres; the alloy compositions should be those representative of refractory high-entropy systems, where the liquid’s complex configuration space is significant.
generation.structural_mediator: The DNN potential’s ability to capture both short- and long-range atomic correlations in the liquid improves the representation of local configurations, thereby mediating a smoother and more continuous energy landscape between reference and target states.
generation.mechanism: By incorporating a wide variety of ab initio liquid configurations in its training, the DNN potential is expected to better reproduce the true potential energy surface. This enhanced fidelity improves phase-space overlap between the integration reference and the target ab initio system, reducing discontinuities (i.e. mismatches) in the thermodynamic integration path.
generation.predicted_outcome: A significant reduction in the mismatch along the thermodynamic integration path relative to TOR-TILD’s EAM references, leading to lower statistical errors in free energy calculations and more accurate prediction of thermodynamic properties.
generation.baseline: Current TOR-TILD methods that rely on EAM potentials, which suffer from insufficient phase-space overlap because they cannot adequately represent the diverse atomic configurations of the ab initio liquid state.
generation.boundary: This improvement is expected for multicomponent, high-melting alloys (such as refractory HEAs) at temperatures near melting; the method may offer diminishing returns in simpler, less compositionally complex systems or at temperatures far below melting.
generation.uncertainty: While a qualitative improvement is anticipated, the exact magnitude of the reduction in integration-path mismatch is uncertain due to limited prior benchmarks in elemental and binary analog systems.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform parallel thermodynamic integration free energy calculations on a selected refractory high-entropy alloy using two reference potentials: one based on the traditional EAM (TOR-TILD) and one based on the new DNN potential. Analyze the integration path for discontinuities and statistically compare the resulting free energy differences.
measurements: Quantitative free energy differences along the thermodynamic integration path
Metrics of phase-space overlap (e.g., distribution of local structural features)
Statistical error margins in the computed free energies
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the DNN-based integration does not demonstrate a statistically significant reduction in the integration-path mismatch (as evidenced by comparable free energy errors or discontinuities similar to those in the EAM-based approach), then the hypothesis is falsified.

Figure 9 shows the calculated lattice parameter and free energy of formation in the considered states and compares them with calculations performed for the composition of the matrix phase of the Ni-based superalloy IN718 found in [] after 8 h of aging at 718 °C.

AbstractHigh-entropy alloys have exhibited unusual materials properties. The stability of equimolar single-phase solid solution of five or more elements is supposedly rare and identifying the existence of such alloys has been challenging because of the vast chemical space of possible combinations. Herein, based on high-throughput density-functional theory calculations, we construct a chemical map of single-phase equimolar high-entropy alloys by investigating over 658,000 equimolar quinary alloys through a binary regular solid-solution model. We identify 30,201 potential single-phase equimolar alloys (5% of the possible combinations) forming mainly in body-centered cubic structures. We unveil the chemistries that are likely to form high-entropy alloys, and identify the complex interplay among mixing enthalpy, intermetallics formation, and melting point that drives the formation of these solid solutions. We demonstrate the power of our method by predicting the existence of two new high-entropy alloys, i.e. the body-centered cubic AlCoMnNiV and the face-centered cubic CoFeMnNiZn, which are successfully synthesized.Subject terms: Materials science, Structure of solids and liquids, Theo

The melting temperature is a crucial property of materials that determines their potential applications in different industrial fields. In this study, we used a deep neural network potential to describe the structure of high-entropy (TiZrTaHfNb)CxN1−x carbonitrides (HECN) in both solid and liquid states. This approach allows us to predict heating and cooling temperatures depending on the nitrogen content to determine the melting temperature and analyze structure changes from atomistic point of view. A steady increase in nitrogen content leads to increasing melting temperature, with a maximum approaching for 25% of nitrogen in the HECN. A careful analysis of pair correlations, together with calculations of entropy in the considered liquid phases of HECNs allows us to explain the origin of the nonlinear enhancement of the melting temperature with increasing nitrogen content. The maximum melting temperature of 3580 ± 30 K belongs to (TiZrTaHfNb)C0.75N0.25 composition. The improved melting behavior of high-entropy compounds by the addition of nitrogen provides a promising way towards modification of thermal properties of functional and constructional materials.
